title: 'Temporary' is a scheduling assumption, not an access-control property: staged code lives at a guessable path under the web root during a maintenance window
index_line: T-0017 · CODE_EXEC · deterministic staging path inside the docroot, reachable between extract and cleanup · php/node/ruby/python · corroborated
invariant_violated: A maintenance routine assumes the window between 'write the new code' and 'move it into place and delete it' is safe because it is short and because the directory is an implementation detail. The directory is inside the document root, its name is deterministic, and the web server executes anything under it. Duration is not a control.

mechanism.does: a routine that must run unattended (full-package upgrade, deploy, installer, cache rebuild) extracts or writes the next version of the application into a staging directory
the staging path is derived deterministically from the package or product name, so it is guessable without any information from the victim
the directory is created beneath the document root, and the web server's execute rule is inherited — the directory carries no access rule of its own
the attacker races: request the deterministic path while the window is open. Nothing in the request is authenticated or unusual
the request is served and executed in the web-server context, before the installer copies files into place and removes the staging area
the fix removes the predictability (randomised staging name), not the window — confirming that guessability was the control being relied on

sync.window.value: the extract→install→cleanup gap; it is a wall-clock window the attacker must hit, so the record is a race, but the guessability is what makes the race winnable at all

source.http.request.value: a plain unauthenticated GET to the staging path — no trigger, no token, no state change; the attacker is a spectator who can act

sink.file.write.value: the staged tree itself: the routine writes attacker-useful code (or core PHP the attacker can drive) into a web-executable location

client.burst.value: request cadence decides whether the race is winnable — poll at the maintenance cadence, or pin the window from an observable side-effect (a version banner changing, a 5xx burst)

preconditions.expr: the web server executes PHP (or the target language) anywhere under the document root, including directories the application created

check.spec: find . -maxdepth 3 -type d \( -name upgrade -o -name staging -o -name tmp -o -name '.deploy*' \) -path '*/public/*' -o -maxdepth 3 -type d -name upgrade 2>/dev/null

preconditions.expr: the staging path is deterministic — derive it from the product and package name and confirm it is the same on every host of that version
an upgrade/deploy can be triggered or is scheduled, and the attacker can observe when it starts
build is in the affected range (WordPress 4.7.0–7.1.3; fixed 7.1.4 randomises the staging path)

success: the same unauthenticated request returns executable output on the vulnerable build and nothing (randomised path) on the fixed build
the response is executed code, not source disclosure: a PHP source file served as text means the execute rule did not apply and the window was not exploitable that way
the request lands inside the -extract/+cleanup interval, evidenced by a version-banner change or a 5xx burst at the same moment
failure_like: the staging path is randomised or carries a nonce — then the request 404s regardless of timing
the staging directory sits outside the document root, or a deny-all rule covers it
false_positive: concluding compromise from a 200 alone: a directory listing or a 404 page also returns 200 in many stacks — require executed output
treating a version banner as proof of the race: banner changes confirm the upgrade happened, not that code was staged at a guessable path
retro-fitting an exploitation claim to a log line without the timing correlation — this is a race, so absence of the correlation is the default

hazards: the window is short and the race real: plan for many attempts and for the maintenance cadence, not a single shot
the write side is the vendor's own code, so there is nothing to upload
the same shape appears in deploy tooling (.git, .svn, release-* directories inside the docroot) where the window is permanent, which is why the class is worth carrying
non_transfers: staging performed outside the document root (a sibling directory, /tmp, a container layer) — nothing to reach over HTTP
stacks whose per-directory execute rule is opt-in rather than inherited — a staged .php is inert there
maintenance modes that also block the staging prefix (a global deny rule during upgrade) — the window closes for the attacker too
